title: Professional economist (integrated degree)
change: Occupational standard and assessment plan revised
overviewOfRole: Producing rigorous, relevant, and impactful economic analysis to drive decision-making at all levels

knowledges.detail: Core economic insights, including that the choices humans make reveal intrinsic value, and that marginal analysis can be used to optimise outcomes and choices across a wide range of problems to maximise human wellbeing through the efficient use of resources.

Microeconomic theory, including the interaction of supply and demand; how markets operate and when they do not work well; how to assess the potential size of a market for a good or service; how individuals and firms make decisions; how firms compete and how industries are structured; how to incorporate realistic assumptions about human behaviour into economic analysis; how to value goods and services, including when their financial value might not be obvious; and how to compare the costs and benefits of different courses of action to inform decision-making.

Macroeconomic theory, including how the economy operates at different levels; what national income and economic growth are, how economists measure them, why they matter, and what drives them; the role of productivity in long-term growth; how to analyse growth trends and productivity drivers using macroeconomic and microeconomic tools; what affects unemployment, wages, and prices; how government policy and international events can affect the economy, and the trade-offs that governments face; inequality and the distribution of income; the role of the financial system in the economy; and broad knowledge of UK economic history.

International economics, including exchange rates; how the economy operates at an international level and the institutions that support it; why and how countries trade; trade policy; and international financial markets.
Economic theory and perspectives, including pluralism and key debates within economics.

The history and application of economic theory, including how economic theory relates to history and institutions, and how this has changed over time; how theory is used in economic policy decisions; the limits of economic theory and economics' interaction with the other social sciences; and how this informs the economic analysis used in the employing organisation.
Statistical and econometric methods for applied economic analysis.
Principles of economic statistics, including how they are constructed, interpreted and applied.
Approaches to selecting and using appropriate statistical software for economic analysis.
Mathematical modelling techniques used to analyse economic problems, forecast trends, and support decision-making.

How bias can affect economic analysis, including cognitive and data-driven biases; the importance of inclusive analysis that serves the whole population; and ethical principles when interpreting and presenting data.
Principles of working safely and securely with digital tools, including cybersecurity, data protection, and the ethical handling of datasets.

Principles of continuous professional development in economics, including research methodologies, publication processes, and knowledge transfer; and emerging fields such as behavioural economics, econometrics, and international trade, recognising their relevance and limitations in relation to the role.

Tools and techniques for managing economic projects, including prioritisation, workflow management, and agile principles; collaborative platforms and shared databases to support research and analysis; and the importance of avoiding reliance on specific branded tools.
The role of emerging technologies in the economy and workplace, including the opportunities and limitations of new digital tools in economic analysis and the associated ethical challenges.
Principles of equity, justice, diversity, and inclusion, and how they impact economic outcomes for people and organisations.

The wider context for economic analysis, including organisational structures; business modelling; global and horizon-scanning perspectives; governance and accountability; technological and policy implications; and the impact of global trends, such as artificial intelligence in the economy, climate change, and sustainability.
Policy evaluation methods and the selection of appropriate methods for assessing economic interventions in different contexts.

behaviours.detail: Demonstrates a questioning and reflective approach in their work.
Shows ownership of work and follows tasks through to completion.
Shows initiative in identifying opportunities to add value.
Responds positively to change and feedback.

Behaves with honesty, integrity, and respect for others in adherence with organisational requirements and professional standards, including the Royal Economic Society (RES) Code of Professional Conduct.
Seeks to improve own performance and ways of working.

skills.detail: Analyse complex information and data, applying economic knowledge to questions of interest while recognising the limitations of economic analysis and available data, and the risks of misunderstanding or misrepresenting economic data.

Use appropriate statistical, econometric, and spreadsheet software to deliver economic analysis, including the efficient and safe use of coding, programming languages, and new and emerging technologies.

Select appropriate analytical approaches from a range of economic and other analytical tools, applying judgement where data is incomplete, and considering context, degree of uncertainty, time pressures, and the question to be addressed, including identifying opportunities where further analysis would add value.

Ensure analysis has impact by understanding decision-makers’ needs, communicating findings and their significance clearly, and proposing actionable recommendations to inform decisions and improve outcomes.
Communicate economic concepts, analysis, advice, risks, and uncertainty clearly and concisely, tailoring communication to the audience to maximise impact.
Listen to, interpret, and understand stakeholders’ needs, including anticipating emerging stakeholder needs, to ensure that economic analysis addresses questions that effectively meet those needs.

Collate evidence from a wide range of sources, assessing the relevance, quality, and validity of research, identifying gaps, bias, and uncertainty, and distilling findings to effectively address the question at hand.

Review and quality assure analysis, ensuring it meets professional and ethical standards; provide constructive challenge to methods, assumptions, evidence, and assess the robustness of conclusions; and evaluate the reliability of new and emerging information technologies, recognising the impact of data quality and bias on performance and accuracy.
Apply judgement to determine when and if simplified or rapid economic analysis is appropriate, identifying and communicating its limitations and risks to decision-makers.
Work to deadlines by planning and prioritising time, coordinating input from others, and responding effectively to changing priorities and requirements, even when under pressure.
Develop and maintain collaborative and professional working relationships to support effective cross-disciplinary and cross-organisational working.
Handle and manage data safely and securely in accordance with relevant protocols and procedures in compliance with legal, ethical, and organisational policies and requirements.

involvedEmployers: Bank of England, Council of the society of professional economists, Department of Business and Trade, Food Standards Agency (FSA), HMRC, Institute for Fiscal Studies, Ministry of Justice, OXERA, UKRI

duties.dutyDetail: Discover what customers, citizens, businesses, or organisations need and how economic analysis can inform their work.
Question and challenge stakeholder briefs to lead, influence, and guide stakeholders in determining the scope of analytical design work.
Support the planning and development of analytical strategies for economic analysis.
Define and conduct research activities, including primary and secondary research using both qualitative and quantitative data, to fully understand users, their needs, and the context of a service.
Gather, select, and analyse data and evidence to support economic analysis.
Identify key themes and seek patterns and insights in research data to identify opportunities for improvement.
Conduct economic analysis of complex information and datasets to develop evidence-based conclusions.
Generate possible solutions by applying an understanding of emerging economic research and developments at the frontier of the discipline to identify innovative approaches to economic problems.
Interpret, review, and reflect on the outcomes of economic analysis, including options and potential recommendations.
Create data visualisations to communicate economic principles, analysis, and recommendations to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
Communicate economic analysis and recommendations to stakeholders.
Test and improve solutions by evaluating ideas, seeking feedback, and making improvements based on user needs and institutional or societal goals.
Evaluate success, measure the impact of changes made, and track progress over time.
Manage and lead ongoing change, supporting long-term improvements by working with influential stakeholders to implement necessary changes.

Manage time and budget to keep projects on track by balancing deadlines, costs, and risks, while keeping the complexity and cost of analysis proportionate to the importance of the issues and decisions being considered.
Support the development of others by helping them acquire the skills needed to contribute to the work through coaching, mentoring, shadowing, collaborative working, or delivering training.
Work effectively with colleagues, stakeholders, and external partners to deliver high-quality economic analysis, encouraging knowledge sharing and interdisciplinary collaboration.

Uphold ethical standards in economic practice and conduct analysis with integrity, transparency, and accountability. Consider the ethical implications of policies to ensure that analysis serves the public interest and accounts for differential impacts across populations.
